title: Bag of Tricks for Image Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks
authors: Tong He, Zhi Zhang, Hang Zhang, Zhongyue Zhang, Junyuan Xie, Mu Li

pages.title: The unsung refinements behind accuracy gains
pages.subtitle: Why the training recipe matters as much as the architecture

blocks.html: The problem. When a new image classifier beats the old record, the headline always credits the architecture — a new kind of layer, a deeper network, a clever connection. But a surprising share of real-world progress comes from quiet refinements in how networks are trained: data-augmentation tweaks, learning-rate schedules, tiny surgical changes to existing blocks. These ‘tricks’ are usually buried in code or mentioned in a single sentence, yet stacked together they rival the gains from a whole new architecture.

Analogy. Imagine two chefs given the identical recipe and ingredients. One follows it literally; the other knows to rest the dough, preheat properly, salt the water, and season in stages. Same dish on paper — wildly different result. This paper is the second chef writing down every technique, and then weighing each one to prove it actually helps.

What the paper does. It does the unglamorous but valuable work of cataloguing these refinements, ablating each one (turning it off to measure its individual contribution), and reporting the cumulative gain on ImageNet. The result is striking: a stock ResNet-50 is pushed from 75.3% to 79.29% top-1 accuracy — better than many newer, fancier architectures — purely by improving the training procedure, with essentially the same network.

By combining these refinements together, we raise ResNet-50's top-1 validation accuracy from 75.3% to 79.29% on ImageNet, and show that improvements transfer to object detection and semantic segmentation.

The three groups of tricks. The refinements fall into: efficient training (large-batch and low-precision tricks that train faster and at least as accurately), model tweaks (small surgical changes to the ResNet downsampling path), and training refinements (schedule and regularization tricks: cosine decay, label smoothing, mixup, distillation).

Context. From the Amazon AWS / MXNet team (Mu Li was a co-creator of MXNet and parameter-server training). It became a much-cited reference precisely because it is a practitioner’s checklist: a single place to find the ‘everyone-knows-this-but-it-is-written-nowhere’ recipe, with numbers attached. The fully-loaded recipe is sometimes called the ‘ResNet-D’ or ‘tricks’ baseline in later work.

pages.title: Large-batch training: warmup and the linear scaling rule
pages.subtitle: Training fast without losing accuracy

blocks.html: The problem. Bigger mini-batches use GPUs more efficiently (more parallel work per step, fewer synchronizations), so you would love to crank up the batch size. But naively, larger batches hurt final accuracy — the model trained with batch 1024 ends up worse than the one trained with batch 256 if you change nothing else. Why, and how do we fix it?

The intuition. A mini-batch gradient is a noisy estimate of the true gradient. A larger batch averages over more examples, so the estimate is less noisy and more trustworthy — which means you can safely take a bigger step. If you keep the same small step, you are wasting the extra confidence and effectively training too slowly.
Trick 1 — Linear scaling rule. Scale the learning rate up in proportion to the batch size:

Reading it: $\eta$ is the learning rate (the step size), $0.1$ is the standard rate that works well for the reference batch size of 256, and $b$ is your actual batch size. So batch 1024 uses $\eta = 0.4$. The rule says: quadruple the batch, quadruple the step. (Introduced by Goyal et al. in the ‘ImageNet in 1 hour’ paper.)

Trick 2 — Learning-rate warmup. At the very start the weights are random, and a large learning rate can send the loss diverging before training stabilizes. So warm up: begin at a tiny rate and ramp it linearly to the target over the first few epochs (e.g. 5). Concretely, if warmup lasts $m$ batches, at batch $i$ use $\eta \cdot i/m$. Let the network find its footing before taking big steps.

items: Zero-γ initialization. Each residual block computes $x + \text{block}(x)$, and the block ends in a BatchNorm layer that scales by a learned $\gamma$. Initialize that final $\gamma$ to 0, so every block starts as the identity $x + 0 = x$. The network then behaves like a shallow net early on — far easier and more stable to train — and gradually ‘turns on’ its depth as $\gamma$ grows.

No bias decay. Weight decay (L2 regularization) is meant to shrink the many weight parameters. Applying it to biases and to BatchNorm’s $\gamma$ and $\beta$ — few in number — just over-regularizes them for no benefit. So decay only the convolution and fully-connected weights, and leave biases and BN parameters alone.

blocks.html: Why it matters / trivia. Together these let the authors train ResNet-50 at batch 1024 with no accuracy loss versus batch 256, unlocking much faster training. Zero-γ init in particular is now a near-universal default for residual networks — a one-line change that meaningfully stabilizes deep training.

pages.title: Low-precision (FP16) training
pages.subtitle: Half the bits, more than the speed

blocks.html: The problem. Networks are traditionally trained in 32-bit floating point (FP16’s big sibling, FP32). But modern GPUs (with tensor cores) run 16-bit floating point (FP16) arithmetic 2–3× faster and use half the memory bandwidth. Can we train in FP16 without wrecking accuracy?

The catch and the fix. Pure FP16 has too little range and precision — small gradients underflow to zero, and tiny weight updates vanish into rounding. The fix is mixed-precision training: do the heavy matrix multiplies in fast FP16, but keep a master copy of the weights in FP32 for stable accumulation, and apply updates there. You get FP16 speed with FP32 stability.

Concrete result. The authors found that switching ResNet-50 to batch size 1024 in FP16 trained much faster — and, somewhat surprisingly, reached marginally higher accuracy than the FP32 baseline (e.g. ~76.2% vs ~75.3% top-1 when combined with the warmup/scaling tricks above). The slight noise from reduced precision may even act as a mild regularizer.

Why it matters. This is the key message of the ‘efficient training’ group: these are not a speed-versus-accuracy tradeoff. You train faster and at least as well. FP16 mixed-precision is now standard practice in essentially all large-scale deep-learning training.

pages.title: ResNet-B, -C, and -D
pages.subtitle: Three small surgical changes to the downsampling path

blocks.html: The problem. The original ResNet has a couple of spots where, by accident of design, it throws away input information during downsampling (the steps that halve the spatial resolution). These tweaks are tiny edits that recover that lost information while barely touching the parameter count or compute.

Concrete example of the waste. In ResNet’s downsampling block, a $1\times1$ convolution is applied with stride 2. A $1\times1$ filter looks at a single pixel; striding it by 2 means it only ever sees one pixel out of every $2\times2 = 4$ — it literally skips three-quarters of the input. That is information lost for nothing.

items: ResNet-B: in the residual path, move the stride-2 from the information-skipping $1\times1$ conv to the following $3\times3$ conv. A $3\times3$ filter with stride 2 still sees every input pixel (its receptive field overlaps), so no information is dropped.

ResNet-C: replace the single expensive $7\times7$ stem convolution at the network’s input with three stacked $3\times3$ convolutions. Same receptive field, fewer multiply-adds, and slightly more accurate (more nonlinearity).

ResNet-D: the shortcut (skip) branch of the downsampling block also uses a $1\times1$ stride-2 conv that drops 3/4 of pixels. ResNet-D inserts a $2\times2$ average-pooling step (stride 2) before the now-stride-1 $1\times1$ conv, so the shortcut downsamples by averaging rather than dropping — keeping all the information.

blocks.html: The gains. Each tweak adds negligible computation but buys a fraction of a percent. Applied together, the fully-tweaked ResNet-D is about 1% top-1 better than the vanilla ResNet-50 at almost no extra cost:

Why it matters / trivia. A ~1% gain for changes that leave the model essentially the same size is an excellent deal. The ResNet-D stem and average-pool shortcut became a de-facto standard — later strong baselines (and timm’s default ResNets) ship with these tweaks built in, often without users realizing the original ResNet differed.

pages.title: Cosine learning-rate decay
pages.subtitle: A smoother schedule than step decay

blocks.html: The problem. The learning rate should be large early (to explore the loss landscape quickly) and small late (to settle precisely into a minimum). The classic step decay does this crudely: keep the rate flat, then divide it by 10 at fixed milestones (say epochs 30, 60, 90). The abrupt drops are jolting and the milestones are arbitrary hyperparameters to tune.
The idea. Cosine decay lowers the rate smoothly along a half-cosine curve, from the initial value down to (near) zero over the whole run — no cliffs, no milestones:

Reading it term by term: $t$ is the current step (or epoch), $T$ is the total number of steps, and $\eta$ is the base (maximum) learning rate. At $t=0$, $\cos(0)=1$ so the factor is $\frac{1}{2}(1+1)=1$ and $\eta_t = \eta$. At $t=T$, $\cos(\pi)=-1$ so the factor is $\frac{1}{2}(1-1)=0$ and $\eta_t = 0$. In between it eases down gently, slowly at first, fastest in the middle, then leveling off near the end.

Why it works. The high rate early explores broadly; the long gentle tail lets the model converge precisely without the abrupt destabilizing jolts of step decay. It also removes the need to hand-pick decay milestones. Empirically it slightly outperforms a well-tuned step schedule (here it contributes the jump to ~77.9% top-1).

Trivia. Cosine decay came from Loshchilov & Hutter’s SGDR (‘warm restarts’) work; this paper helped popularize the single-cycle, no-restart version that is now the default schedule in countless training recipes.

pages.title: Label smoothing, mixup, and knowledge distillation
pages.subtitle: Regularizing the targets and the training data

blocks.html: The shared problem. Standard training pushes the model toward over-confidence: with a hard one-hot label, the cross-entropy loss is only minimized when the model predicts probability 1.0 for the true class and 0.0 for all others — an impossible, infinitely-confident target that encourages the logits to blow up and hurts generalization and calibration. These three tricks all soften the training signal.

Label smoothing. Replace the hard target 1 with $1-\varepsilon$ and spread the remaining $\varepsilon$ mass uniformly over the other classes. For $K$ classes, the true class gets $1-\varepsilon$ and each other class gets $\varepsilon/(K-1)$ (the paper uses $\varepsilon=0.1$). The model now aims for a slightly softened distribution, stays better calibrated, and its feature clusters become tighter and more separated.
Mixup. Train on convex blends of pairs of examples and their labels. Given two samples $(x_i, y_i)$ and $(x_j, y_j)$, form a new training point:

Reading it: $\lambda \in [0,1]$ is drawn from a Beta distribution each step; $\hat{x}$ is a pixel-wise blend of two images (a faint ghost of a cat over a dog), and $\hat{y}$ is the same blend of their one-hot labels (e.g. 0.7 dog, 0.3 cat). This forces linear behavior between examples, smooths the decision boundary, and improves robustness — but because each ‘image’ is harder, it benefits from training longer (the paper goes from 120 to 200 epochs).

Knowledge distillation. Train the ResNet-50 student to match not only the true labels but also the soft predictions of a stronger, more accurate teacher (here a ResNet-152). The teacher’s softened probabilities carry ‘dark knowledge’ — e.g. that a particular truck image also looks a bit like a bus — which the student absorbs via a distillation term (a temperature-scaled cross-entropy against the teacher’s outputs) added to the normal loss.

Trivia. All three were existing ideas (label smoothing from Inception-v3/Szegedy 2016; mixup from Zhang et al. 2017; distillation from Hinton et al. 2015). The paper’s contribution is showing they stack cleanly with each other and with the schedule/architecture tricks on a single strong ResNet baseline.

The heart of the paper. Any single trick is easy to dismiss as noise. The persuasive evidence is the progression: start from a baseline ResNet-50 and switch on the refinements one at a time, watching top-1 ImageNet accuracy climb monotonically. This is the table practitioners actually cite.

rows: + Efficient training (batch 1024, FP16, warmup, zero-γ, no-bias-decay)

blocks.html: Reading the trajectory. No single line is dramatic — the biggest single jump is the ~1% from ResNet-D. But they accumulate to roughly a 4-point top-1 gain (75.3% → 79.29%), turning a stock ResNet-50 into a model competitive with much newer architectures, without changing the fundamental network. (Note: distillation’s benefit interacts with the others — it helps less once mixup and a strong teacher recipe are present.)

Why it matters. This is the paper’s thesis made quantitative: the training recipe is worth as much as several years of architecture search. It reframes ‘a fair comparison’ — you cannot credit a new architecture for beating an under-trained ResNet baseline, because half the gap may just be tricks the new model happened to use.

pages.title: Transfer and takeaways
pages.subtitle: The gains are not just ImageNet trivia

blocks.html: The worry. A skeptic could argue these tricks merely overfit the ImageNet classification benchmark — squeezing out validation points that mean nothing for real use. If so, the improved backbones would not help on other tasks.

The evidence against it. The authors take the trick-trained ResNet-50 backbone and drop it into downstream systems. On object detection (Faster R-CNN on PASCAL VOC) and semantic segmentation (FCN on ADE20K), the better-trained backbone yields better mAP and mIoU than the vanilla one. Better features in, better results out — so the refinements produce genuinely better representations, not benchmark-specific quirks.

items: Training procedure matters as much as architecture; small, well-known tricks compound into large gains.
Efficient training: linear LR scaling, warmup, zero-γ init, no-bias-decay, and FP16 mixed-precision — faster and at least as accurate.
Model tweaks: ResNet-B/C/D fix information loss in the stem and downsampling blocks for ~1% at almost no cost.
Training refinements: cosine LR decay, label smoothing, mixup, and knowledge distillation.
Cumulatively: ResNet-50 goes from 75.3% to 79.29% top-1 on ImageNet, and the gains transfer to detection and segmentation.

blocks.html: Lasting influence. This paper became a standard citation for ‘train your baseline properly before claiming an architecture win’, and its recipe directly shaped the default training pipelines in libraries like GluonCV and timm. Many of its tricks — cosine decay, label smoothing, mixup, zero-γ, FP16 — are now simply how everyone trains.
